title: Bioinformatics Module | Bioinformatics and Drug Design
text:
General InformationTP Classes OverviewWeekly Schedule


This 9-week module introduces bioinformatics concepts and tools relevant for pharmaceutical sciences. Students will gain hands-on experience with public databases and online tools to retrieve, analyse, and interpret molecular databases.
Format:

Weekly: 1-hour theory class + 1.5-hour practical class (repeated for 2 student groups).

Target audience: Pharmacy students with introductory knowledge in molecular biology and genetics.
Evaluation:


Participation in class is welcome, and will be positively evaluated.


The details related to the final evaluation format will be discussed and agreed with the students. Either:


A final written exam; or
A video (3 minutes maximum; in groups of 5 students) + oral presentation (10 min) of one drug target (explored in at least 3 of the molecular databases covered in class).









Goal
Learn to independently explore and critically interpret bioinformatics resources in order to connect drugs with their molecular targets and understand their pharmacological, mechanistic, and clinical relevance.


Learning outcomes
By the end of the TP practical classes, students should be able to:

Identify the molecular target(s) of a given drug using authoritative online bioinformatics resources.
Retrieve and interpret relevant molecular information on drug classes, mechanisms of action, target function, 3D structure, and clinical associations.
Integrate data from multiple sources to explain the pharmacological and clinical importance of a drug–target pair.
Demonstrate independent inquiry skills by selecting appropriate databases, justifying search strategies, and reflecting on findings.
Communicate discoveries clearly through concise answers.



TP Activities overview
The students will have access to a hands-on guided tutorial to learn how to explore online resources in order to uncover information that is central to pharmaceutical sciences students.
The following databases will be covered:

Ensembl = gene identity, functional details, and Genome browsing
UniProt = protein details
PDB = protein structure
Drug bank = drug details
ClinPGx = clinical pharmacogenomics
Opentargets = therapeutic drug targets

























Topic 1 | Introduction to Bioinformatics and Biological Databases

Lecture Topics:

Definition and scope of bioinformatics.
Bioinformatics in drug discovery.
Overview of databases per biological data types.
Primary and secondary databases.
Bioinformatics as an experimental science: search, compare, model, and integrate data.

TP Activity:

Introductory hands-on tutorial from EBI: Bioinformatics for the terrified





Topic 2 | Genes, Genomes, and Regulation

Database: Ensembl
Lecture topics

Navigating the Ensembl genome browser
Understanding gene structure (exons, introns, UTRs, CDS)
Finding and exploring gene variants

Learning goals

Learn to locate a gene in a genome browser.
Retrieve basic genomic information such as chromosomal position and gene structure.
Interpret visual representations of genes and transcripts.

TP Activity

Part 1: Introductory video + Hands-on tutorial
Part 2: Hands-on tutorial (continuation)





Topic 3 | Proteins

Database: UniProt,
Lecture topics

Accessing protein annotation, domains, and sequence features
Exploring the rich network of external links to complement protein information

Learning goals

Learn to retrieve and interpret protein functional information.
Use UniProt as and entry point to integrate information from variuous sources.

TP Activity

Hands-on tutorial.

Database: PDB
Lecture topics

Visualising protein structures
Exploring ligand binding sites in protein complexes

Learning goals

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
ImportantAttribution and licence



The exercises in this lesson are adapted from the Ensembl browser training material produced by EMBL-EBI and the Ensembl team, which is made available under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence.

Source: Ensembl training materials, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/ensembl-browser-series/.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
Overview






NoteQuestions this lesson answers




How do you find a gene in Ensembl and read its Gene tab?
What is the difference between all annotated transcripts, protein-coding transcripts, and the MANE Select transcript?
Where do phenotype, disease, and Gene Ontology annotations appear, and where do they come from?
How do you inspect exons, untranslated regions, cross-references, and expression probes for a single transcript?
How do you start from a disease and work back to a gene?
How do you navigate, configure, and export a genomic region?
How do you read allele frequencies, ancestral alleles, and conservation for a SNP?
How do you predict the consequences of a structural variant with VEP?









TipLearning objectives



By the end of this session you should be able to:

Search Ensembl by gene name, by phenotype, and by genomic coordinates.
Choose an appropriate transcript for downstream work, and justify the choice.
Turn browser tracks on and off, and export sequence in FASTA format.
Interpret population genetics, conservation, and phenotype association data for a variant.
Run the Variant Effect Predictor on a structural variant and filter the results.




Practical details






Time estimate
~1.5 hours (5 exercises, roughly 15 to 20 minutes each)


Level
Introductory


Prerequisites
Genes, transcripts, exons, UTRs, and the idea of a reference genome


Software needed
A web browser only









Ensembl publishes a new release several times a year, and annotation changes between releases. Transcript counts, transcript names, identifier versions, and even the set of associated phenotypes may differ from the answers given here. Treat any mismatch as a discussion point rather than a mistake: ask students which release they are looking at, and where that information is displayed on the page.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
section: 1 Exploring the MYH9 gene in human
text:
1 Exploring the MYH9 gene in human
MYH9 encodes myosin heavy chain 9, a non-muscle myosin.

1.1 Locating the gene






Tip🔬 Hands on




Go to https://www.ensembl.org.
Select Human from the species drop-down list.
Type MYH9 in the search box and click Go.
Click MYH9 (Human Gene) in the results to land on the Gene tab.









Warning❓ Question




Which chromosome and which strand is the gene on?
How many transcripts (splice variants) are annotated, and how many are protein coding?
Which is the longest protein-coding transcript, and how long is the protein it encodes?
Which transcript would you take forward for further study, and why?







NoteShow answer






Chromosome 22, on the reverse strand.
23 transcripts, of which 6 are protein coding.
MYH9-215, encoding a protein of 1,981 amino acids.
MYH9-201, because it is the MANE Select transcript. MANE Select transcripts are agreed between Ensembl and RefSeq as the single representative transcript for a gene, with matching sequences in both databases, which makes results easier to compare across resources. Hover over the MANE Select flag in the transcript table for the definition.












NoteWhy “longest” and “best” are not the same thing





Note that the longest protein-coding transcript (MYH9-215) is not the one we choose to work with. Length is a poor proxy for biological relevance.
Ask yourself: What would you do if a gene had no MANE Select transcript? What evidence should you look for instead? (Hint: look at the expression support, protein evidence, TSL, and APPRIS flags in the transcript table).





1.2 Phenotypes






Tip🔬 Hands on




Click Phenotypes in the left-hand panel.
The table is long. Type MIM in the filter box at the top right to keep only entries from Mendelian Inheritance in Man.









Warning❓ Question



Are any diseases associated with this gene according to MIM?






NoteShow answer





Yes, several. Two examples are deafness (autosomal dominant 17) and macrothrombocytopenia with granulocyte inclusions, with or without nephritis or sensorineural hearing loss. Click any record for more detail.







1.3 Gene Ontology
The Gene Ontology project annotates gene products in three separate namespaces: biological process, cellular component, and molecular function.






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click GO: Biological process in the left-hand panel.








Warning❓ Question



What functions is MYH9 annotated with?






NoteShow answer





Angiogenesis, cell adhesion, and protein transport are among the biological processes listed. Note that all of the GO terms here are attached to a single transcript, ENST00000216181.







1.4 Inside one transcript






Tip🔬 Hands on




In the transcript table, click the transcript ID for MYH9-201 (ENST00000216181) to move to the Transcript tab.
Click Exons in the left-hand panel.
Then click General identifiers in the left-hand panel.









Warning❓ Question




How many exons does this transcript have?
Are any exons completely or partially untranslated?
Is there a matching sequence in UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot?







NoteShow answer






41 exons, as reported in the transcript summary.
Exon 1 is completely untranslated, and exons 2 and 41 are partially untranslated. UTR sequence is shown in orange. The cDNA view in the left-hand panel shows the same thing in sequence form.
Yes: P35579.254 in UniProt/Swiss-Prot matches the translation of this Ensembl transcript. Click the accession to jump to UniProtKB, or click align to see the alignment.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
section: 2 Finding a gene associated with a phenotype
text:
2 Finding a gene associated with a phenotype
Phenylketonuria is a genetic disorder in which phenylalanine cannot be metabolised in any body tissue. Phenylalanine accumulates, causing seizures and intellectual disability. Here we work in the opposite direction to the previous exercise: from the disease to the gene.






Tip🔬 Hands on




Go to the Ensembl homepage.
Type phenylketonuria in the search box and click Go.
Narrow the results to Gene using the left-hand menu.









Warning❓ Question



Which gene is associated with this disorder?






NoteShow answer





PAH, phenylalanine hydroxylase, ENSG00000171759.











Tip🔬 Hands on: compare the transcripts




If the transcript table is hidden, click Show transcript table.
Click Transcript comparison in the left-hand menu.
Click Select transcripts, then either tick each protein-coding transcript in turn or use the drop-down and choose Protein coding.
Close the menu to see the comparison.









Warning❓ Question



How many protein-coding transcripts does PAH have?






NoteShow answer





Six.











Tip🔬 Hands on: cross-references and structure




Click External references in the left-hand menu.
Then open the transcript table, click the MANE Select ID (ENST00000553106.6), and choose PDB 3D protein model in the left-hand menu.









Warning❓ Question




What is the MIM gene identifier for PAH?
In the model 2pah, how many protein molecules can you see?







NoteShow answer









Two. The model 2pah is shown by default; rotate it if the second chain is not obvious at first.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
3 Exploring a genomic region
This exercise moves from gene-centric to coordinate-centric browsing.






Tip🔬 Hands on: navigate to the region




Go to the Ensembl homepage and select Human.
Type the coordinates in the search box and click Go:
13:32264000-32492000









Warning❓ Question




On which cytogenetic band does this region sit?
How many contigs make up this part of the assembly?







NoteShow answer






Band q13.1.
Three, shown by the alternating light and dark blue bars in the Contigs track. A contig is a contiguous stretch of sequence assembled from direct sequencing information alone.












Tip🔬 Hands on: zoom in on BRCA2



Drag a box with the mouse around the BRCA2 transcripts, then choose Jump to region from the pop-up menu.








Tip🔬 Hands on: add the LTR repeat track




Click Configure this page in the side menu, or the cog wheel icon at the top left of the lower image.
Go to Repeats in the left-hand menu and select LTR.
Click the (i) button to read the track information.
Save and close with ✓, or by clicking outside the pop-up.









Warning❓ Question




Which tool was used to annotate the LTRs?
How many LTRs fall within BRCA2, and do any overlap exons?







NoteShow answer






RepeatMasker.
Ten LTRs overlap BRCA2, and none of them overlaps an exon.












Tip🔬 Hands on: export the sequence




Click Export data in the side menu.
Leave the defaults (FASTA sequence should already be selected) and click Next.
Click Text.









Warning❓ Question



What information does the FASTA header carry?






NoteShow answer





The assembly, the sequence type, the chromosome, the start and end coordinates, and the strand. For example:
>13_dna:chromosome_chromosome:GRCh38:13:32311910:32405865:1
This is worth dwelling on: coordinates are meaningless without an assembly version, and a FASTA file that does not record one is a liability in any project.











Tip🔬 Hands on: tidy up



Click Configure this page, then Reset configuration, then ✓. This turns off every track you added, so the next exercise starts from the default view.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
4 Population genetics and phenotype data
The SNP rs1738074, in the 5’ UTR of the human TAGAP gene, has been reported as a genetic risk factor for several diseases.






Tip🔬 Hands on: find the variant



There is more than one route. Either:

open the Variation table for the human TAGAP gene and use the Consequence filter to keep only 5’ UTR variants, or
search Ensembl directly for rs1738074.

Once you are on the Variant tab, click Genes and regulation in the menu.








Warning❓ Question



In which transcripts is this SNP found?






NoteShow answer





In four transcripts of TAGAP. It is also an intron variant of one lncRNA transcript of TAGAP-AS1.











Tip🔬 Hands on: allele frequencies



Click Population genetics in the left-hand panel (or click Explore this variant and then the Population genetics icon).








Warning❓ Question



What is the least frequent genotype in the Yoruba (YRI) population from 1000 Genomes phase 3?






NoteShow answer





CC, at a frequency of 5.6%.











Tip🔬 Hands on: conservation




Click Phylogenetic context in the left-hand panel.
Click Select an alignment, open Multiple alignments, choose 91 eutherian mammals EPO-Extended, and click Apply.









Warning❓ Question




What is the ancestral allele, and how was it determined?
Is it conserved across the eutherian mammals?







NoteShow answer






The ancestral allele is T, inferred from the alignment in primates.
The view centres the SNP (highlighted in red) with its flanking sequence. The T allele is conserved in all but two of the eutherian mammals shown.












Tip🔬 Hands on: phenotype associations



Click Phenotype data in the left-hand panel.








Warning❓ Question



Which diseases is this SNP associated with, and are risk alleles reported?






NoteShow answer





Multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and white blood cell count. Risk alleles and the corresponding P values are given for all three.
Watch the strand. The allele A is reported as associated with celiac disease, and G appears for multiple sclerosis, yet Ensembl lists the alleles for this variant as T/C. Ensembl always reports alleles on the forward strand, so the original publications must have reported theirs on the reverse strand. This is a common and easily missed source of error when combining variant data from different sources.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
section: 5 VEP analysis of a structural variant
text:
5 VEP analysis of a structural variant
A breast cancer sample carries a genomic deletion, described here in VCF format:
13  32307062    sv1 .   <DEL>   .   .   SVTYPE=DEL;END=32908738






Tip🔬 Hands on: run VEP




Click VEP at the top of any Ensembl page and open the web interface.
Check that the species is Human.
Give the job a descriptive name, for example Patient deletion exercise. Naming jobs is a good habit: it is how you tell results apart later, and the name is what appears in the browser when you view the data.
Paste the variant into the Paste data field and click Run.









Warning❓ Question



How many genes are affected?






NoteShow answer





Twelve.











Tip🔬 Hands on: filter the results



At the top of the results table, add the filter Consequence is transcript_ablation and click Add.








Warning❓ Question



Does the deletion remove any complete transcripts?






NoteShow answer





Yes. Complete transcripts are lost for PDS5B, N4BP2L1, BRCA2, RNY1P4, IFIT1P1, ATP8A2P2, N4BP2L2, and N4BP2L2-IT2, plus one gene with no official symbol, ENSG00000212293.











Tip🔬 Hands on: view it in the browser



Click the location link in the results table, 13:32307062-32908738. This opens Region in detail in a new tab. If you named the job, the data appears automatically in red. If not, use Configure this page and add it under the Personal data tab.








Warning❓ Question



You saw part of this region already in Section 3. What does the deletion do to BRCA2, and why might that matter in a breast cancer sample?






NoteShow answer





The deletion spans the whole of BRCA2, so the gene is lost entirely rather than altered. BRCA2 is a tumour suppressor involved in homologous recombination repair, so complete loss is a far more consequential event than a single missense change, and it is the kind of variant that a SNV-focused pipeline can easily miss.
This question is an addition to the original exercise set; drop it if you are short of time.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
Key points






TipTake home messages




Ensembl can be entered from three directions: a gene name, a phenotype, or a set of coordinates. All three converge on the same annotation.
A gene usually has many transcripts. Pick one deliberately, and prefer MANE Select where it exists.
Left-hand panel links (Phenotypes, GO, Exons, General identifiers, Oligo probes) are where the cross-references live.
Genomic coordinates mean nothing without an assembly version, and alleles mean nothing without a strand.
VEP scales the same reasoning up from single bases to structural variants, and its consequence filters are how you find the events that matter.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts
text:
Exercises to extend the session






NoteSuggested follow-up




Repeat the first exercise for a gene of your own choosing and report the transcript you would take forward, with reasons.
Take P35579 from the MYH9 General identifiers page into the UniProt lesson and compare what each database tells you about the same molecule.
Use BioMart to export the exon coordinates of all protein-coding transcripts of PAH as a TSV file.
Construct a VCF line for a deletion of your own and predict, before running VEP, which consequence terms it should return.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
ImportantAttribution and licence



This lesson is adapted from “One protein along the UniProt page” by Lisanna Paladin and Bérénice Batut, Galaxy Training Network, published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. Original material: https://gxy.io/GTN:T00360.
The text below has been rewritten and reorganised for this course. Any errors introduced in adaptation are mine, not the original authors’.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
Overview






NoteQuestions this lesson answers




How can you search for proteins by free text, gene name, or protein name?
How do you read the information at the top of a UniProt entry page?
What kind of information sits behind each download format (FASTA, JSON, XML, GFF)?
How is the function of a protein such as an opsin described?
What structured information lives in the Names and Taxonomy, Subcellular location, Disease & Variants, and PTM/Processing sections?
How do you find expression, interaction, structure, family, sequence, and similarity data?
What do the Variant viewer and Feature viewer tabs add?
What does the Publications tab list, and how can it be filtered?
Why does the annotation history of an entry matter?









TipLearning objectives



By the end of this session you should be able to:

Interpret a UniProtKB entry: function, taxonomy, localisation, structure, interactions, and variants.
Use stable unique identifiers to move between databases.
Download protein data in an appropriate format for a downstream task.
Visualise and compare sequence features along a protein.




Practical details






Time estimate
~1 hour


Level
Introductory


Prerequisites
Basic familiarity with genes, proteins, and FASTA files


Software needed
A web browser only









Numbers reported in the solutions below (counts of search hits, publications, variants, and so on) were correct when the lesson was written. UniProt is updated roughly every eight weeks, so your numbers may differ. That is a feature, not a bug.
Ask yourself: Why does a knowledge base change?

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
1 Why bother with UniProt?
A typical analysis ends with a shortlist of interesting proteins. Then what? You need to find out what those proteins do, where they act, what is already known about their variants, and which other databases hold complementary information.
This lesson uses human opsins as a worked example. Opsins sit in the cells of the retina, where they capture light and start the signalling cascade that produces vision. When they are disrupted, the result can be colour blindness or other visual impairment.
Almost all of the work happens on the UniProt website rather than in any analysis platform, so nothing needs installing.






NoteSources and further reading





The original Galaxy Training Network lesson drew on the UniProt help page Explore UniProtKB entry, and chose the topic following Gale Rhodes’ Bioinformatics Tutorial. The latter can no longer be followed step by step (the resources have changed too much) but is still a good source of background on opsins and on building structural models from evolutionary information.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
2 Finding the right entry
The starting point for protein annotation is UniProtKB. You can query it with free text, a gene name, or a protein name. Let us begin with something deliberately vague.






Tip🔬 Hands on: a broad search




Open https://www.uniprot.org/.
Type Human opsin into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question



How many results come back?






NoteShow answer





Around 524 at the time of writing. Far too many to inspect by hand, even though (spoiler) the entry we want is near the top.





Free text is too blunt an instrument. A better strategy is to search on a unique identifier. The gene we are after is OPN1LW.






Tip🔬 Hands on: search by gene name




Type OPN1LW into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question




How many results now?
What is still missing from the query?







NoteShow answer






Over 240 results.
The organism. The same gene name is used across many species, so add Human to restrict the search.












Tip🔬 Hands on: search by gene name plus organism




Type Human OPN1LW into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question




How many results now?
Is there a hit whose gene name is exactly OPN1LW?







NoteShow answer






Eight results.
Yes. The first hit carries the label Gene: OPN1LW (RCP).






That first hit, P04000 (OPSR_HUMAN), is our target. Two things are worth noticing before opening it:

The protein name (OPSR_HUMAN) and the gene name (OPN1LW) are different, and so are their identifiers. Gene and protein are distinct entities with distinct names.
The entry carries a gold star, meaning it has been manually annotated and curated by a human (Swiss-Prot) rather than generated automatically (via TrEMBL).

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
3 Reading the entry page






Tip🔬 Hands on: open the entry



Click on P04000 · OPSR_HUMAN, or go directly to https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04000/entry.








Figure 1: The header of a UniProt entry page. Image from the Galaxy Training Network lesson, CC BY 4.0.




The page is long, so the left-hand navigation bar does a lot of work. It stays fixed as you scroll, and just reading it tells you what the database holds about this entry:



known functions
taxonomy
subcellular location
variants and associated diseases
post-translational modifications (PTMs)




expression
interactions
structure
domains and their classification
sequences and similar proteins



At the very top of the page you get the accession and entry name, the protein and gene names, the organism, whether the entry has been reviewed by a curator, an annotation score, and the evidence level for the protein’s existence.
Below the header sit six tabs: Entry, Variant viewer, Feature viewer, Publications, External links, and History. Stay on Entry for now.

3.1 Downloading the entry
Just under the tabs there is a toolbar. From here you can BLAST the sequence, align it against its isoforms, add the entry to a basket for later, or download it.






Warning❓ Question




Which formats does the Download menu offer?
What sort of information does each one carry?







NoteShow answer






Text, FASTA (canonical), FASTA (canonical and isoform), JSON, XML, RDF/XML, and GFF.
The FASTA options give you the sequence, optionally as a multi-FASTA that includes isoforms. The rest are general-purpose structured formats, not biology-specific: they carry the same annotation you are reading on the page, but in a form that a script can parse. JSON is usually the most convenient for programmatic work.








3.2 Function
The Function section opens with a short free-text summary: visual pigments are the light-absorbing molecules behind vision, and consist of an apoprotein (opsin) covalently bound to cis-retinal.
Two sentences to stand in for decades of literature. That compression is possible because someone has already done the curation work, and because the protein has been classified in the Gene Ontology (GO), which describes molecular function, biological process, and cellular component.
GO is a good example of a resource that flattens a very complex body of knowledge into a graph. Detail is lost, but in exchange the information becomes countable, comparable, and machine-readable, which is exactly what makes summary pages like this one possible.






Warning❓ Question



Which GO terms is this protein annotated with, for:

molecular function?
cellular component?
biological process?







NoteShow answer






Photoreceptor protein, G-protein coupled receptor.
Photoreceptor disc membrane.
Sensory transduction, vision.








3.3 Names and taxonomy
The next section holds more structured information, including the taxonomic placement of the protein. It also lists other identifiers that point at the same biological entity, or at linked entities (for example associated diseases under MIM).






Warning❓ Question




What is the taxonomic identifier?
What is the proteome identifier?







NoteShow answer






9606, that is Homo sapiens.
UP000005640, and this protein is a component of chromosome X.








3.4 Subcellular location
We already know where the protein is in the body (the retina). Where is it in the cell?






Warning❓ Question




Where does UniProt place this protein within the cell?
Is that consistent with the GO annotation you saw earlier?







NoteShow answer






It is described as a multi-pass membrane protein: it is embedded in the membrane and crosses it several times.
Yes. GO is more specific, naming the photoreceptor disc membrane.






This section also has a Features area showing which stretches of the sequence sit inside the membrane (transmembrane) and which do not (topological domain).






Warning❓ Question



How many transmembrane and topological domains are listed?






NoteShow answer





Eight transmembrane regions and seven topological domains.







3.5 Disease and variants
This gene and protein are linked to several diseases. The section describes those associations and lists the specific variants implicated in each.






Warning❓ Question



What kinds of study establish that a genetic variant is associated with a disease?






NoteShow answer





Three common designs:

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Scan whole genomes across large cohorts to find common variants that track with a trait or disease.
Case-control studies. Compare the frequency of specific variants between affected and unaffected individuals.
Family studies. Follow inheritance patterns within families in which several members are affected, which can pinpoint candidate genes.

All of these lean heavily on genomic file formats such as SAM, BAM, and VCF.





A Features area maps the natural variants along the sequence, and points you to the fuller view in the Variant viewer tab. Resist the temptation for now.


3.6 PTM and processing
A post-translational modification is a covalent event after translation: either a proteolytic cleavage, or the addition of a chemical group to an amino acid.






Warning❓ Question



Which post-translational modifications are annotated here?






NoteShow answer





Chain, glycosylation, disulfide bond, and modified residue.







3.7 Expression
For human proteins there is often tissue-level expression information, drawn from resources such as the Expression Atlas.






Warning❓ Question



In which tissue is this protein found?






NoteShow answer





The three colour pigments are found in the cone photoreceptor cells.







3.8 Interaction
Proteins do their work by interacting with their surroundings, and above all with other proteins. This section lists known interactors in a table you can filter by subcellular location, disease, and interaction type. Much of the underlying data comes from databases such as STRING, which is linked directly.






Tip🔬 Hands on: follow the link out to STRING



Open the STRING network for this protein in a new tab.








Warning❓ Question




How many download formats does STRING offer?
What does each one carry?







NoteShow answer





STRING exports interaction data in several shapes:

TSV, a tabular layout that drops straight into analysis tools.
PSI-MI XML, a community standard for interaction data, which makes the results interoperable with other interaction databases.
PNG and SVG images of the network, for slides and figures.
Flat files with detailed interaction evidence, and multiple alignment files for comparing sequences across the network.








3.9 Structure
The Structure section is the way into the three-dimensional world. It reports experimentally determined structures where they exist, and gives you an interactive viewer embedded in the page, so you can rotate the molecule and explore domains, binding sites, and other functional regions without leaving UniProt.






Warning❓ Question




Which variant is associated with colour blindness?
Can you locate that amino acid in the structure?
Why might that substitution be disruptive?







NoteShow answer






From the Disease & Variants section: a glycine to glutamic acid change at position 338.
Yes. Rotate the model and hover over residues to find position 338. It takes patience given how many helices there are. Residue 338 is not in a helix, but in what looks like a loop, just before a region of low prediction confidence.
A reasonable hypothesis: since it is not in a helix, and helices in transmembrane proteins are usually the membrane-spanning parts, this residue is in one of the larger domains protruding from the membrane. So the mutation probably disturbs a functional domain rather than the membrane-embedded core. Use the Feature viewer to check whether that domain faces the inside or the outside of the cell.






Where does the model actually come from?






Tip🔬 Hands on: download the structure




Click the download icon underneath the structure viewer.
Open the downloaded file in a text editor and look at the first few lines.



You get a PDB file, describing the arrangement of atoms and residues. But notice that the list of 3D structure databases does not link to the Protein Data Bank first. It links to AlphaFoldDB.
That matters. This is a predicted structure, not an experimentally determined one. AlphaFold infers the spatial arrangement of atoms using deep learning and evolutionary information. It is also why the model is coloured by confidence: blue regions are predicted reliably, orange regions are either uncertain or genuinely disordered (flexible and mobile). The file format is the same as for an experimental structure, because the information it encodes is still structural, but the epistemic status is very different.






ImportantTeaching note





This is a good moment to stop and discuss provenance with students. Two files can look identical in format while differing completely in how much you should trust them. Ask: how would you record that distinction in your own project metadata?





3.10 Family and domains
This section places the protein in its evolutionary context: the families, superfamilies, and domains it belongs to, plus conserved regions, motifs, and other notable sequence features.
The Features area confirms that at least one of the two protruding domains (the N-terminal one) is disordered, and reiterates that we are dealing with a transmembrane protein. The links out to phylogenetic and domain databases are the route into questions of common ancestry and functional specialisation.


3.11 Sequence
Everything above is ultimately encoded in the sequence. Here you can download the FASTA file, trace the data back to the sequencing experiments that produced it, and see any isoforms that have been detected.






Warning❓ Question



How many potential isoforms map to this entry?






NoteShow answer





One: H0Y622.







3.12 Similar proteins
The final section of the Entry tab lists similar proteins, produced by clustering at 100%, 90%, and 50% identity thresholds.






Warning❓ Question



How many similar proteins are there at each threshold?






NoteShow answer

A pattern should be emerging: much of what we do with protein data is mapping different layers of information onto the same sequence and asking how they relate. The next two tabs do exactly that, visually.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
4 Variant viewer






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Variant viewer tab.


This view maps every known alternative version of the sequence. Some have a known effect (pathogenic or benign); many do not.






Warning❓ Question



How many variants are flagged as likely pathogenic?






NoteShow answer





Zoom out and count the red points: five.





The sheer number of variants is a useful corrective. A “protein sequence” (like a gene sequence, or a structure) is much less of a fixed object than the singular canonical entry suggests.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
5 Feature viewer






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Feature viewer tab.


The Feature viewer merges all the Features areas scattered through the Entry page into one track-based display: domains and sites, molecule processing, PTMs, topology, proteomics, and variants. Clicking a feature highlights the corresponding region in the structure.






Tip🔬 Hands on: locate the variant in context




Expand the Variants track.
Zoom out.
Click the red point at position 338.









Warning❓ Question



What is the topology at that position?






NoteShow answer





It falls in a topological cytoplasmic domain, so on the inside of the cell. This also answers the open question from Section 3.9.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
6 Publications






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Publications tab.


This tab lists papers relevant to the protein, combining a manually curated list (from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot) with automatically imported references. You can filter by source, by the category of data a paper contributes (function, interaction, sequence, and so on), and by study size (small scale versus large scale).






Warning❓ Question




How many publications are linked to this protein?
How many of them contribute information about its function?







NoteShow answer

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
7 External links






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the External links tab.


This tab gathers every cross-reference scattered across the entry into one place. The link text usually shows the identifier that represents the same entity in the other database, which is what makes automated cross-referencing possible at all.
For a sense of how tangled that web is, look at the bioDBnet network diagram (source). Databases are the major nodes, identifiers the minor ones, and the region around the UniProt entry name, Gene ID, and Ensembl Gene ID is extremely dense. The diagram is already partly out of date, which rather makes the point.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
8 History






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the History tab.


The History tab exposes every previous version of the entry’s annotation, in this case going back to 1988, and lets you download them. It is a record of how knowledge about this protein has accumulated and been revised.






Warning❓ Question



Was this entry ever not manually annotated?






NoteShow answer





Scroll back through the table and check the Database column. It never sits in TrEMBL, only in Swiss-Prot, so the entry has been manually curated from the start.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
Key points






TipTake home messages




UniProtKB entries collect function, taxonomy, localisation, interactions, and much more in one curated place.
Search on unique identifiers, not free text, whenever you can.
The Variant viewer and Feature viewer let you see variants, domains, modifications, and topology mapped onto the sequence.
External links and shared identifiers are what let you cross-reference between resources.
The History tab shows that annotation is a moving target, not a fixed fact.

text:
Exercises to extend the session






NoteSuggested follow-up (edit or remove these for your own course)




Repeat the whole walk-through for OPN1MW (medium-wave opsin) or RHO (rhodopsin) and note where the entries differ in evidence level and annotation score.
Download the JSON for P04000 and write a short script that extracts every annotated transmembrane region as a table.
Compare the AlphaFold model with an experimentally determined GPCR structure of your choice. Where do the confidence estimates and the experimental data agree?
Pick one paper from the Publications tab and trace which annotations in the entry it supports.
